title: IMF Backs India's Revised GDP Method, Calls Update Welcome Development
excerpt: Krishna Srinivasan said in Bangkok the new base and method match IMF statistics advice, as the Fund raised India's growth outlook to 7%.
body:
• The IMF said on Thursday in Bangkok that India's updated GDP methodology is consistent with good practice and with advice from the IMF's own statistics department.
  • Asia and Pacific Director Krishna Srinivasan called the base revision a welcome development and credited MoSPI's work on GDP statistics.
  • The endorsement follows a domestic dispute over 7.8% April-June growth, which a former finance secretary said was flattered by revisions to the prior year.
  • For investors, the IMF also raised India's growth outlook to 7% this year and next, with about 6.9% over the medium term, and said rupee pressure is not a sign of economic failure.

The International Monetary Fund has backed India's revised method for calculating gross domestic product, saying the update aligns with international best practice. Speaking to reporters in Bangkok on Thursday, Krishna Srinivasan, director of the IMF's Asia and Pacific Department, called the GDP base revision a welcome development and said it matched advice the Fund's statistics department had given India.

"These revisions to the methodology are entirely consistent with what the advice we've been giving them."

— Krishna Srinivasan, IMF Asia and Pacific Director

Srinivasan said India had also published a note explaining the revisions, and he credited the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation, known as MoSPI, for improving GDP statistics, while adding there is always room for further improvement. His remarks were reported by The Hindu BusinessLine.

Why methodology became a political argument

The endorsement lands after a row over India's better-than-expected 7.8% growth for the April-June quarter. Former Finance Secretary S. C. Garg argued the figure was boosted by compressing the previous year's numbers, a claim opposition parties took up to question the integrity of official data. Chief Economic Adviser V. Anantha Nageshwaran rejected that reading as cherry-picking and explained the latest figures use the financial year ending March 2023 as the new base, with the methodology change revising last year's quarterly data.

That context is what makes an outside referee matter. GDP is not a survey opinion; it is built from production, income and expenditure series whose base year determines what the economy is weighted to look like. An outdated base overweights shrinking sectors and misses new activity. The IMF's position — that what India did is consistent with good practice — does not settle every argument about a single quarter, but it does validate the framework those quarters are now calculated in.

Growth outlook and the rupee

The methodology comments came alongside a broader assessment. According to BizzBuzz's IANS report of the same Bangkok briefing, the IMF has raised India's growth outlook to 7% for this year and next, with a medium-term trajectory around 6.9%, citing resilient domestic demand, strong services activity, favourable demographics and ongoing structural reforms in its World Economic Outlook.

Srinivasan also addressed currency pressure. India entered the recent energy shock with strong fundamentals and responded well, he said, and pressure on the rupee should not be read as economic failure. Exchange rates, he noted, are a function of global interest rates, investor risk appetite and oil prices. The IMF's Regional Economic Outlook for Asia and the Pacific, released Thursday, listed India among emerging economies that faced currency pressure after the energy shock, noted that pressure has partly eased in recent months, and recorded India among economies that intervened in foreign exchange markets.

What this means for readers

For diaspora investors comparing Indian and US assets, the practical takeaway is narrower than the headline praise. The IMF is certifying the measuring stick, not guaranteeing any quarter's print: future GDP releases on the new base should be more comparable with peer economies and with the Fund's own forecasts, which now sit at 7%. Scrutiny will continue — Srinivasan himself flagged room for improvement — but challenges to Indian growth data will now have to argue against the method the IMF says it recommended.
